Okay, something everyone claims but is getting wrong, automation this time around is not going to create new jobs. In the past, the new jobs were necessary because automation still needed humans to monitor and work the machines. That's not the case in this day and age because computer programs can run those machines flawlessly and do the work humans would have normally done. The only jobs this would create are the singular supervisor jobs that will only require 1-5 people max, repair jobs which may not last long as robots can be created to come in and fix any malfunctions within minutes and get the robot back up and running, and a slight few others that would only require up to a few thousand people (which isn't even 0.001% of the entire human population). Also, AI is already reaching a point of self learning and being able to program itself and upgrade itself without any human interaction, and that's in 2022. This means in 10 years time, ai will be doing the things you claim humans will be needed for.

AI is a different paradigm, especially when combined with robotics. Not today’s AI, but in the near future. Today’s AI is just a very smart parrot that is capable of mimicking behavior, but we aren’t far off from true AI, capable of making predictions, coming to decisions based on those predictions, and taking appropriate actions far faster and more accurately than humans. Combine that with near future robotics and they will be capable of doing any job humans can do, only better and faster. With no time off. In some cases they will be able to do jobs humans can’t, because they don’t need to be anthropomorphic. Imagine a lawn care service where a drone drips off a few robots, they mow the lawn, rake the leaves, trim the hedges, put down seed and fertilizer only where needed, remove the weeds at the root, and then the drone picks them up and takes them to the next job. Or a stock trader that exists solely on a server and can make trades in less than a quarter of a second. The only things that are safe involve physical talents like sports players, trades that protect themselves like movie stars and screen writers, and those with power to self protect like politicians, lawyers, and government bureaucrats.

So first of all, great insightful video. There are definitely places where I feel like I have a differing opinion, but I'm glad to see someone spell out the process in a clear and concise way, and that my belief that "vibe coding" (prompt and forget) isn't realistic for production environments is at the very least a shared belief in this case. And to be clear, I'm not saying LLMs can't be useful, I just find myself not using them past finding features in libraries I use, or generating tooling that helps me directly. I feel like what puts me and others off from this process is a few core beliefs that probably aren't shared by everyone, so I'll list them. 1. Deeply understanding code through reading is *significantly* harder than through writing. 2. Describing a problem in enough words to get it exactly right, short of writing the entire solution in actual code and giving it to the AI, is practically impossible (read: you need to make significant compromises in order to accept the machine output outright). 3. True solutions often come from building something and finding out some minutia that doesn't work, re-evaluating the solution, and trying again. My experience with AI is that it will just bulldoze through bad assumptions and implement it anyway, and you may become blind to how those changes make the API worse, because you didn't have to use it. Often I hear people suggest you define the API first and then let the AI make the implementation, but it's incredibly rare that the first API my team comes up with is the one we end with because of several unseen factors that only become apparent after either my colleagues have been exposed to it or after I've gotten far enough in implementing it. 4. Even if we assume that a perfect engineer is capable of generating and understanding all code like this as fast or faster than hand-rolling code, not everyone is a perfect engineer. I think that a "less than stellar" engineer can do more harm with AI tools that are capable of spitting out code faster than they can think about it. And sure, review is meant to catch that, but it becomes a pain that's offloaded to others especially when people feel more inclined to not argue about their code and just delegate it to "the AI told me this is a good solution". Might be an extreme case, but based on experience I feel that it's realistic. With these things in mind, I have a really hard time seeing how *I* could be more productive with more agentic tools than I already use. I feel that somewhere, somehow, I have to give up something that I consider essential to good software. In essence when people tell me (and this doesn't have to be true for you) that they generated code and understand it fully, I generally don't believe that that's completely true. When they wrote it I could assume the answer was most likely yes, but now it's a guess, and the more "productive" they are the bigger the doubt is. Maybe for small snippets or single functions it doesn't make a huge difference, but entire features? Entire codebases? I'm not even saying it's feasible to fully understand all code in a project on Meta's scale when coding by hand either, but I think that it's much easier to understand and to take ownership of significant portions of it. Essentially, I feel like I've been driving a car normally for 15 years now, and suddenly a new hot trend has emerged: foot steering. Some of the biggest names in driving are putting out statements on how it was hard at first, but they've finally driven 5 miles with their foot-driven workflow and their hands are now completely free to do other things! And the further people go with this process the more convinced people become that "wow, I didn't think driving with your feet was possible, maybe this really is the future". But I can't wrap my head around it, because you'd still arrive at the same destination, following the speed limit hopefully, using a process that's hard to learn and prone to make huge mistakes, and the benefits of having your "hands free" seem to not outweigh the downsides of not having control over your vehicle. Yeah, super contrived example I'm sure lol. But that's how it feels to me, maybe there's some insights that you have on where you overcome these problems.

I see CS as jack of all trades. You'll pick up the basics of all sorts of concepts, from networks to databases to cybersec, architecures, AI and coding. Imo if you dont know what you want to do or you see value in all of this, its a great option. Software engineering is focused towards the process of building software, coding, methodologies, architecturing, designing, UML, etc. Also it may still vary depending on location/country and university. I did systems engineering and the program was very similar to a bachelor's in CS from the US. Theyve since renamed the programs in universities across my country and now they offer IT and Software Engineering. Usually you'll still need to take required math, like physics and calculus. Point is, do your research and see what the program is like. Choosing either doesnt normally really block your career paths and its up to you to then specialize when working
